data.name: Tennis Elbow 2013
data.detailed_description:
Created by and for tennis fans, Tennis Elbow 2013 is a tennis simulation with an easy and intuitive learning curve, but with exceptional gameplay depth.

In this tennis game, you'll have to show all your tactical skills, use an iron mind and quick reflexes, as well as a sharp eye to guess the ball trajectories, all of this to choose your next strike wisely.

To beat your opponent, you have the choice between all the possible strikes on a real court, from the safe strike to the acceleration, including the drop shot and the topspin lob.

This tennis simulation is designed for all tennis lovers, whether gamepad mashers or keyboard novices, because of its numerous difficulty levels. In addition, a visual help system will assist you in aiming the ball and positioning your player. You can turn these options on and off whenever it suits you.

TE2013 features one of the most complete World Tour ever made in a tennis video game. With 3000 players evolving over 36 years, competing in 300 tournaments each year, from the low rank tournament qualifications to the top level event finals, both in singles and doubles competition, you’ll feel like diving in a real professional tennis player’s career.

Tennis Elbow game engine is very open to modifications and TE2013 has an active Modding community.

Features:
  • 9 different court surfaces : clay, green clay, grass, hard, blue-green hard, classic synthetic, NewLine synthetic, indoor hard and indoor synthetic; each with a specific rebound
  • 300 tournaments, with 3500 players evolving over 38 years
  • The Country Cup
  • Singles & doubles competitions
  • 6 difficulty levels, each split in 10 sublevels
  • Full ranking system
  • 3D male & female players fully customizable
  • Singles, 3, and doubles games
  • Split screen
  • Network : LAN and online games (only available on the Windows version, not on the Mac OSX & Linux versions)
  • 1 to 6 games per set, in best of 1, 3 or 5 sets
  • 7 camera modes
  • Game is very Modding friendly

Warning:
You can play doubles with 4 human players on 1 computer, or on 2 computers with 2 players per computer by LAN or Internet, but not on 4 computers.

Copyright 2008-2015 Emmanuel Rivoire. This item is not authorized for posting on Steam, except under the Steam account named ManuTOO.

reviews.review:
Tennis Elbow 2013 is a tennis simulation built around the idea that believable mechanics and tactical depth matter more than spectacular presentation. Developed and published by Mana Games, it delivers a surprisingly detailed interpretation of the sport despite its visibly dated graphics. Instead of relying on flashy animations or elaborate broadcast effects, the experience concentrates on movement, positioning, timing, shot preparation, and reading an opponent. This approach gives matches a methodical quality that becomes increasingly rewarding as the player learns how its systems interact.

The gameplay provides considerably more depth than its straightforward controls initially suggest. Players can use different types of strokes for offensive and defensive situations, including powerful acceleration shots, safer returns, topspin lobs, and drop shots. Positioning is especially important because simply pressing the correct shot button does not guarantee an effective return. Reaching the ball early, preparing properly, choosing an appropriate direction, and understanding the opponent's position all influence the outcome. As a result, longer rallies often become tactical contests where patience and intelligent placement can be more valuable than raw power.

An extensive difficulty system helps make this simulation approachable. Six major difficulty levels are divided into numerous sublevels, allowing the challenge to increase gradually rather than forcing players into large jumps in opponent ability. Visual assistance can help newcomers understand positioning and aiming, while experienced players can reduce these aids for a more demanding experience. This flexible structure makes it possible to learn the mechanics progressively while still providing substantial challenge for players who already understand tennis strategy.

The World Tour mode is one of the strongest reasons to invest significant time in the game. Rather than presenting isolated tournaments, it simulates a large professional circuit containing thousands of competitors and hundreds of events. Players can create a tennis professional and attempt to climb the rankings through increasingly difficult competition. Singles and doubles events are available, while rankings and tournament progression create a convincing sense of building a career. The sheer scale of the tour helps make individual victories meaningful, particularly when a developing player begins reaching later rounds against stronger opposition.

Court surfaces provide another layer of strategy. Nine different surface types are represented, covering variations of clay, grass, hard courts, synthetic surfaces, and indoor conditions. The ball behaves differently depending on the court, meaning a strategy that works comfortably in one tournament may require adjustment in another. Differences in rebound behavior affect timing and positioning, encouraging players to understand each environment rather than treating surfaces as simple visual changes.

Match customization is similarly extensive. Singles and doubles are supported, match lengths can be adjusted, and several camera perspectives allow players to find a viewpoint that suits their preferences. Local split-screen competition is available, while network functionality expands the experience beyond computer-controlled opponents. Character customization is relatively modest by modern standards, but it provides enough flexibility to establish a personal competitor for the career modes. Modding support is another significant advantage, particularly for players interested in extending or altering the game's content.

Presentation is the area where its age is most apparent. Character models and environments are functional rather than impressive, animations occasionally appear stiff, and the interface has a distinctly older PC-game character. Anyone approaching it expecting the production quality of a contemporary big-budget sports title may find the first impression underwhelming. Audio is similarly restrained, emphasizing basic match atmosphere rather than elaborate commentary or television-style presentation. However, the relatively lightweight visuals also help the game run on modest hardware.

Steam Deck compatibility is not officially rated by Valve, so it should be considered Unverified rather than formally Verified or Unsupported. Its relatively modest hardware demands are encouraging, but the absence of an official compatibility rating means handheld users should expect that controls, interface navigation, text readability, or other aspects may require adjustment. Players specifically purchasing it for Steam Deck should therefore approach it as an unofficial rather than guaranteed handheld experience.

Where the game ultimately succeeds is in making improvement feel meaningful. Early matches can expose poor positioning and careless shot selection, but experience gradually teaches players how to construct points, anticipate returns, change direction intelligently, defend under pressure, and recognize opportunities to attack. Winning becomes satisfying because progress is closely connected to understanding tennis rather than simply improving character statistics.

Tennis Elbow 2013 remains an appealing choice for players who prioritize simulation, career depth, tactical rallies, surface variation, and customization over modern visual polish. Its presentation has aged considerably, but the underlying tennis mechanics remain unusually substantial. The enormous career structure and scalable difficulty also provide excellent longevity. For someone willing to accept its old-fashioned appearance, it offers a thoughtful and highly replayable interpretation of competitive tennis.

Rating: 8/10
